```{r}
#| echo: false
library(tidyverse)
library(lintr)
library(styler)
library(biometrydata)

big <- function(x){ format(round(x), big.mark = ",") }
avo <- avonet

# what lint() and style_text() say about one messy line
messy_line <- "MeanMass=mean(x,na.rm=T)"
lint_demo <- as.data.frame(lint(text = messy_line))
styled_line <- as.character(style_text(messy_line))

# the hawks exercise
hawks <- avo |>
  filter(Family1 == "Accipitridae")
mean_hawk_mass <- mean(hawks$Mass, na.rm = TRUE)
habitat_summary <- hawks |>
  group_by(Habitat) |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(Mass),
            mean_wing = mean(Wing.Length))

messy_hawks <- paste0('Hawks=avo|>filter(Family1=="Accipitridae")\n',
                      'MeanMass<-mean(Hawks$Mass,na.rm=T)\n',
                      'Hawks|>group_by(Habitat)|>summarise(m=mean(Mass),',
                      'w=mean(Wing.Length))->HabitatSummary\n')
n_lint_messy <- length(lint(text = messy_hawks))

# wide and long
avo_wide <- avo |>
  select(Species1, Mass, Wing.Length, Beak.Width, Beak.Length_Culmen)
avo_long <- avo_wide |>
  pivot_longer(cols = Mass:Beak.Length_Culmen,
               names_to = "trait",
               values_to = "trait_value")

# bobwhite, made wide
bw_wide <- bobwhite_counts |>
  select(route, year, count) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = count)
n_empty <- sum(is.na(bw_wide))
bw_back <- bw_wide |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -route, names_to = "year", values_to = "count")
bw_back_drop <- bw_wide |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -route, names_to = "year", values_to = "count",
               values_drop_na = TRUE)

# pseudocode examples
beak_top <- avo |>
  mutate(delta_beak_length = Beak.Length_Culmen - Beak.Length_Nares) |>
  mutate(mass_corrected_delta_beak_length = delta_beak_length / Mass) |>
  slice_max(order_by = mass_corrected_delta_beak_length, n = 1)
pointy <- avo |>
  group_by(Family1) |>
  filter(n() >= 10) |>
  summarise(mean_hwi = mean(Hand.Wing.Index, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_hwi))
```

## Part 1: the code {.smaller}

A **full analysis**, not a fragment:

- loading the data
- any transformations, and the reason for them
- the code behind any modeling decision you made
- the model itself
- the figures

. . .

**Fully reproducible and well documented.** Someone else should be able to run
it and get your results. The rest of today is how.

::: {.notes}
"Reproducible" has a specific meaning here, and it is the one from Assignment 2:
someone else, on another machine, with your code and your data, gets your
numbers.

The most common failure is an absolute path to their own Desktop. The second is
data that only exists on their laptop. Dec 1 (reproducibility) covers both.
:::

## Part 2: the writing {.smaller}

An updated draft of your midterm writing, same three sections:

- **Introduction**: the question, and why it matters
- **Methods**: the data, and what you did to it
- **Results**: including the results of a **statistical model**, not just plots

. . .

Figures should be better than the midterm's. You know ggplot2 now.

::: {.notes}
The upgrade from the midterm is the model. At midterm they were plotting; now
they fit something and report it.

Remind them that the text is theirs: the syllabus allows AI for code, not for
the writing in this section. That comes up again on Tuesday, in getting help.

Good comments make the Methods section easy to write; the comments section at
the end of today shows how.
:::

## Part 3: the presentation {.smaller}

About **five minutes**, during the final exam block, all from **one shared
Google Slides file**: add your slides to it before the session. The link will
be on Canvas.

A format that works:

- Title slide
- Background, 1 to 2 slides: what is your question, why does it matter
- Methods, 1 to 2 slides
- Results, 1 to 2 slides
- What you would do next

::: {.notes}
Five minutes is short. The commonest mistake is three slides of background and
no results.

Why one file: nobody spends their five minutes getting a laptop to talk to the
projector, and talks follow each other without a gap. The link goes on Canvas
only, never on these slides or in the assignment, because both are public and
anyone with the link could edit the file. Ask them to check their slides in
the shared file beforehand, since things pasted from PowerPoint can shift.
:::

## Presenting well {.smaller}

- **Minimize text.** Roughly seven lines, seven words each, as an upper bound
- **Practice the timing**, out loud, with a clock
- **Going long costs points**, because it takes time from the next speaker

. . .

Your figures are the presentation. If a figure needs a paragraph of explanation,
fix the figure.

::: {.notes}
The 7x7 rule is a ceiling and not a target. Most good slides have less.

If anyone wants to go further on figures, the figures supplement covers
palettes, combining panels, and plotting model predictions.
:::

# Code style

## Why style matters {.smaller}

Your code will be read by:

- **future you**, in three weeks, writing the final project
- **me**, grading Assignment 4 and the final project
- **anyone you ask for help** (Tuesday's lecture): a forum, a labmate, a chatbot
- **reviewers and readers**, if you share it with a paper

. . .

Consistent style lets a reader see the **logic** instead of decoding the
**layout**. Some style rules also prevent real bugs, as you will see.

::: {.plain}
Code is read far more often than it is written, so write it for the reader.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. R for Data Science chapter 4 follows the tidyverse style guide
(style.tidyverse.org), and that is the one we use. Other style guides exist
(Google's, for one); the rule that matters most is to pick one and be
consistent.
:::

## Get set up {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
library(lintr)        # checks your style: install it first if you need to
library(styler)       # fixes your spacing: install it first if you need to
library(biometrydata)

avo <- avonet         # all 11,009 bird species, as in Lectures 23 and 24
nrow(avo)
```
:::

**Check:** `r big(nrow(avo))` rows.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. lintr and styler are both on CRAN. The old version of this
lecture read AVONET from a URL; the course package has it, so no internet is
needed.
:::

## File names {.smaller}

| Rule | Good | Bad |
|---|---|---|
| lowercase **snake case**: words joined by `_` | `avonet_traits.csv` | `BirdData.csv` |
| letters, numbers, `_` and `.` only | `bobwhite_counts.csv` | `Bird data?.csv` |
| describe what is inside | `clean_bobwhite.R` | `script2.R` |
| number files that run in order, with a leading 0 | `01_download.R`, `02_clean.R` | `1_download.R`, ..., `10_plot.R` |
| dates as year, month, day | `avonet_clean_20261119.rds` | `avonet_clean_11-19-26.rds` |
| no "final" | `report_v2.docx` | `report_FINAL_really.docx` |

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Why each one:

- Spaces and symbols break file paths in code and on some operating systems;
  `?` is not even allowed in a Windows file name.
- Without a leading zero, 10_plot.R sorts before 2_clean.R.
- Year-month-day dates sort in time order alphabetically; other orders do not.
- "Final" is never final. Git keeps the history, so one file
  name is enough; if you must keep versions, number or date them.

Ask: of avonet_bird_trait_data.csv, BirdData.csv and Bird data?.csv, which is
best, and what is wrong with the other two?
:::

## Object names {.smaller}

- **Snake case**, lowercase: `parrot_data`, `mean_mass`
- Objects are **nouns**: `hawks`, `habitat_summary`
- Functions are **verbs**: `plot_wing_shape()`, `load_bbs_data()`
- **Long and clear beats short and cryptic**: autocomplete does the typing
- Related objects share a **prefix**: `avonet_parrots`, `avonet_tits`

. . .

**Quick:** name an object holding the penguins (Spheniscidae). A function that
turns AVONET into family averages?

::: {.notes}
Three minutes, with the question to the room. Good answers: penguins or
avonet_penguins; family_means() is fine, summarize_by_family() is clearer. Forest
birds: forest_birds.

Bolker and older R code use dots (words.separated), and so do AVONET's own
columns (Wing.Length). Leave column names you did not make alone unless you
have a reason; name your own things in snake case.
:::

## Why names matter: three tries {.smaller}

```{r}
parrot_data <- avo |> filter(Family1 == "Psittacidae")
nrow(parrot_data)
```

```{r}
#| error: true
parrot-data <- avo |> filter(Family1 == "Psittacidae")
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
parrot data <- avo |> filter(Family1 == "Psittacidae")
# Error: unexpected symbol in "parrot data"
```

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. The first works. The second is read as "parrot minus data", and R
complains that there is no object called parrot. The third does not even parse.
Both errors are about the name, not the filtering, which is exactly why they are
confusing when you meet them in your own code.
:::

## Do not reuse R's own names {.smaller}

```{r}
T <- 0                          # a reasonable name for a temperature...
mean(c(4, NA, 6), na.rm = T)    # ...and now na.rm = T means na.rm = 0
rm(T)
```

. . .

- Write **`TRUE` and `FALSE`** in full: `T` and `F` are ordinary names anyone can overwrite
- Avoid naming things `data`, `c`, `mean` or `t`: they are already functions

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. The point to land: a style rule can be a bug fix. T is just a
variable that R sets to TRUE at startup; nothing stops you from changing it.
TRUE cannot be overwritten. lintr flags every T and F for this reason.

data <- read.csv(...) does work, because R finds the function data() when it
needs a function, but it makes error messages confusing ("object of type
'closure' is not subsettable" is the classic one, met on Tuesday).
:::

## Spaces {.smaller}

| Do | Not |
|---|---|
| `a <- 1 + 2` | `a<-1+2` |
| `b <- 2^3` | `b <- 2 ^ 3` |
| `mean(x = avo$Mass, na.rm = TRUE)` | `mean( x=avo$Mass,na.rm=TRUE )` |
| `avo$Mass >= 100 & avo$Habitat == "Forest"` | `avo$Mass>=100&avo$Habitat=="Forest"` |

- Spaces around `<-`, `=`, `+`, `==`, `&` and friends; **not** around `^`, `$` or `:`
- A space **after** each comma, none just inside parentheses
- Extra spaces to **line things up** are fine

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. Spaces can also change meaning: x<-3 assigns 3 to x, but x < -3
asks whether x is less than minus 3. The spaced version is never ambiguous.

The alignment point is from the old slides: lining up the = signs in a long
summarise() call is allowed, and many people find it easier to scan.
:::

## Pipes and arguments {.smaller}

```{r}
#| eval: false
family_summary <- avo |>
  group_by(Family1) |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(Mass),
            sd_mass = sd(Mass),
            mean_wing_length = mean(Wing.Length))
```

- `|>` goes at the **end** of a line, and each step starts a new line
- Named arguments that do not fit on one line get **one line each**
- Assign with `<-` at the **start**, not `->` at the end
- ggplot2's `+` follows the **same rules** as `|>`
- A pipe longer than about **10 lines**: break it into named steps

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Why each:

- One step per line reads like a recipe, and you can comment out one step to
  see what it does.
- One argument per line makes a missing comma easy to spot.
- `->` at the end reads naturally ("and call the result family_summary"), but
  someone scanning the left edge of your script for where family_summary was
  made will never find it. The tidyverse guide advises against it for that reason.
- ggplot2 predates the pipe, so it chains layers with + instead; lay them out
  the same way, one layer per line with + at the end.
- A very long pipe is hard to check: if the answer is wrong, you cannot see
  where. Save the result after a big change of shape (a summarise() or a
  pivot) under a name that says what it holds, and start a new pipe from it.
  R for Data Science chapter 4 suggests 10 to 15 lines as the point to split.

RStudio indents for you: select the code and press Ctrl+I (Cmd+I on a Mac).
:::

## Sections {.smaller}

Long scripts need **signposts**. Ctrl+Shift+R (Cmd+Shift+R on a Mac) inserts one:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# load the data ------------------------------------------------------------
```

- RStudio lists sections in the **outline** (the button at the top right of the
  script), so you can jump between them
- Leave a **blank line** between steps that do different things

**Try it now:** add a section label to your script for today's code.

::: {.notes}
One minute. Any comment ending in four or more dashes, equals signs or pound
signs counts as a section; Ctrl+Shift+R just types it for you. For the final
project, good sections are the same as the Methods section's paragraphs: load,
clean, fit, compare, plot.
:::

## Let R check your style {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
lint(text = "MeanMass=mean(x,na.rm=T)")         # lintr: lists the problems
style_text("MeanMass=mean(x,na.rm=T)")          # styler: fixes what it can
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(data.frame(lint_says = lint_demo$message))
```

`style_text()` gives `` `r styled_line` ``: spacing fixed, but **not the name or the
`T`**. Those need you.

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Typing code in as text is only for seeing what the two packages
do; the next slide is how they are really used.

Why I prefer lintr: it tells you, and you decide. styler changes things
silently, and it cannot fix anything that needs judgment, like a name. There are
some style conventions I ignore, and with lintr I can see them and move on.
:::

## In practice: point them at your files {.smaller}

Nobody types their code into `lint()`. You point it at a **script**, or a
whole **folder** of them:

```{r}
#| eval: false
lint("scripts/02_fit_models.R")   # one script: problems by line number
lint_dir("scripts")               # every R script in a folder

style_file("scripts/02_fit_models.R")   # restyles that file, in place
style_dir("scripts")                    # ... and every file in the folder
```

- In RStudio, the **Addins** menu has "Lint current file" and "Style active
  file", for the script you have open
- `lint()` results open in the **Markers** pane: click one to jump to that line
- `style_file()` and `style_dir()` **overwrite** your files: commit or copy first

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Paths are relative to the project folder, as for data files.
lint_dir() and style_dir() also look inside subfolders, and pick up R Markdown
and Quarto files as well as .R scripts.

The usual rhythm: lint the file you are working on before you share it or hand
it in. Running style_dir() on a whole project rewrites everything at once,
which makes a git diff very hard to read, so do that once at the start, not
in the middle of a project.

To switch off a rule you disagree with, put a file called .lintr in the
project folder. For example, to allow lines up to 120 characters:

    linters: linters_with_defaults(line_length_linter(120))

The Addins menu is the button labelled Addins in RStudio's toolbar; both
packages install their entries when installed.
:::

## Your turn: restyle the hawks {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

This works, but it is hard to read:

```{r}
#| eval: false
Hawks=avo|>filter(Family1=="Accipitridae")
MeanMass<-mean(Hawks$Mass,na.rm=T)
Hawks|>group_by(Habitat)|>summarise(m=mean(Mass),w=mean(Wing.Length))->HabitatSummary
```

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# Open a new script (File > New File > R Script) and save it as hawks.R.
# Rewrite the three lines above in good style, with clear names.
# Then check it (or use Addins > Lint current file):
# lint("hawks.R")
```
:::

**Check:** `lint()` finds nothing. `r nrow(hawks)` hawk species, average mass
`r big(mean_hawk_mass)` g, a summary row for each of `r nrow(habitat_summary)` habitats.

::: {.notes}
Eight minutes, in pairs. The original gets `r n_lint_messy` lint notes. One clean version:

hawks <- avo |>
  filter(Family1 == "Accipitridae")
mean_hawk_mass <- mean(hawks$Mass, na.rm = TRUE)
habitat_summary <- hawks |>
  group_by(Habitat) |>
  summarise(mean_mass = mean(Mass),
            mean_wing = mean(Wing.Length))

If lint() says "Missing terminal newline", put the cursor after the last line
and press Enter: RStudio does not add one by default.

The names are the part styler could not do: m and w say nothing, mean_mass and
mean_wing say everything. The rock-dwelling species are the heaviest (five
eagles and vultures, including the bearded vulture); the 138 forest species are
the lightest.
:::

# Data style

## Wide and long {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Wide:** one row per species

```{r}
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(head(avo_wide[, c("Species1", "Mass", "Wing.Length")], 2))
```

Good for entering data and reading by eye
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Long:** one row per measurement

```{r}
#| echo: false
long3 <- avo_wide |>
  select(Species1, Mass, Wing.Length) |>
  head(2) |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(Mass, Wing.Length),
               names_to = "trait", values_to = "trait_value")
knitr::kable(long3)
```

Good for plotting many traits at once, and adding new kinds of measurement
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. The same numbers, two shapes. Neither is wrong; which one you
want depends on what you are about to do with it. Most of the time, for
tidyverse functions and for models, the answer is the one where each row is
one observation, which the next slide defines.
:::

## Tidy data {.smaller}

Three rules (R for Data Science, chapter 5):

1. Each **variable** is a column
2. Each **observation** is a row
3. Each **value** is a cell

. . .

- `bobwhite_counts` is tidy: one row per route per year, which is exactly what
  `glmer()` needed on Tuesday
- What counts as "an observation" depends on your question, so there can be
  more than one tidy version of the same data

::: {.plain}
Tidy data puts one observation in each row, so every tidyverse function, and
every model, knows where to find things.
:::

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Ask: is avo_wide tidy? Yes, if the question is about species: a
species is the observation and each trait is a variable. If the question is
about measurements (say, plotting every trait's distribution), the long version
is the tidy one.

The commonest untidy data in ecology: one column per year (count_2019,
count_2020, ...), one column per site, or two values in one cell ("12/15").
:::

## Entering data: rules for spreadsheets {.smaller}

From Broman and Woo (2018), *Data organization in spreadsheets*, for anyone
entering field or lab data:

- **Be consistent:** one code per thing (`female`, not `F`, `f` and `Female`), one name per site
- **Missing is `NA`:** never -999, and never a blank, which could be a slip
- **Dates as YYYY-MM-DD**
- **One thing per cell:** mass in one column with its unit in the column name, not "12.4 g"
- **A rectangle:** one header row, no merged cells, no calculations or graphs
- **No color or bold as data:** if a highlight means something, make it a column
- **A data dictionary:** what each column is, its units, how it was measured
- **Never edit the raw file:** save a CSV copy, back it up, and clean it in code

::: {.notes}
Four minutes. Neither reading covers this, and it is where most biologists'
data problems start: in the spreadsheet, before R is involved. The paper is
Broman, K. W., and Woo, K. H. (2018), The American Statistician 72(1): 2 to 10,
https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2017.1375989. It is open access, short, and
worth assigning to anyone collecting data. Its twelve rules; the slide skips
"choose good names" (the file and object names slides cover it) and folds
backups, plain-text copies and "no calculations" into the last two lines. The
last, data validation in Excel, is worth a mention to anyone entering data by
hand: it restricts a column to numbers in a range or a list of codes.

Why each:

- Inconsistent codes become separate groups in R: "F" and "f" are two sexes to
  group_by().
- A -999 for "not measured" gets averaged in as a real value. If a file
  already uses one, read_csv(..., na = c("", "NA", "-999")) fixes it on the way
  in. A blank is ambiguous: missing on purpose, or never typed? The paper
  prefers every cell filled; White et al. (2013) prefer blanks, so the one rule
  everyone agrees on is to pick one code and use it everywhere. Notes on why a
  value is missing go in their own column, not in the cell.
- Excel converts anything that looks like a date. Ziemann et al. (2016) found
  gene-name errors, mostly from this, in 20% of gene lists in journals'
  supplementary files. Year-month-day is unambiguous and sorts correctly; the
  paper suggests storing dates as text, or as separate year, month and day
  columns, so Excel leaves them alone.
- A merged cell, a second header row or a calculation breaks the rectangle that
  read_csv() expects. Do calculations and graphs in a copy, or better, in R.
- Color does not survive saving as CSV, and R cannot see it.
- The data dictionary is most of the final project's Methods paragraph on the
  data.
- Never editing the raw file is Part 1 of the final project: the cleaning
  is in the script, so it is reproducible. The paper says to write-protect the
  raw file, back it up in more than one place, and keep a plain-text (CSV)
  copy, which any program can read forever.
:::

## Make it long: `pivot_longer()` {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
avo_wide <- avo |>
  select(Species1, Mass, Wing.Length, Beak.Width, Beak.Length_Culmen)

avo_long <- avo_wide |>
  pivot_longer(cols = Mass:Beak.Length_Culmen,   # the columns to stack
               names_to = "trait",              # their names go here
               values_to = "trait_value")       # their values go here
avo_long
```
:::

**Check:** `r big(nrow(avo_wide))` rows become `r big(nrow(avo_long))`: how many
per species, and why?

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Four per species, one for each trait stacked. The three
arguments are the whole idea: which columns, where their names go, where their
values go.
:::

## Why long? Every trait in one plot {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.2
ggplot(avo_long, aes(x = trait_value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~ trait, scales = "free")
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. With the wide data this would be four separate plots. In the long
data, trait is a variable, so ggplot can split by it. This is the main reason
to make data long: ggplot2 and group_by() work on variables, not on column
names.
:::

## And back: `pivot_wider()` {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
avo_wide2 <- avo_long |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = Species1,       # what identifies a row
              names_from = trait,      # new column names come from here
              values_from = trait_value)

all.equal(as.data.frame(avo_wide2), avo_wide)
```
:::

**Check:** `TRUE`: nothing was lost on the way there and back.

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. as.data.frame() because pivot_wider() returns a tibble and avonet
is a plain data frame; without it, all.equal() reports the difference in class,
not in content.
:::

## Your turn: bobwhite, one column per year {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
bw_wide <- bobwhite_counts |>
  select(route, year, count)
  # make it wide: one row per route, one column per year (hint: pivot_wider())

# how many cells are empty? (hint: is.na() and sum())

# for anyone fast: make bw_wide long again, with and without values_drop_na = TRUE.
# Then try pivot_wider() with only year and count selected. What goes wrong?
```
:::

**Check:** `r nrow(bw_wide)` rows and `r ncol(bw_wide)` columns, with
`r big(n_empty)` empty cells. Back to long: `r big(nrow(bw_back))` rows, or
`r big(nrow(bw_back_drop))` with `values_drop_na = TRUE`.

**Then:** which version is easier to read by eye? Which one could `glmer()` use?

::: {.notes}
Seven minutes, in pairs. The answer:

bw_wide <- bobwhite_counts |>
  select(route, year, count) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = count)
sum(is.na(bw_wide))

The wide table is how a field crew might keep it, and it shows the gaps
plainly: each NA is a route-year missing from these data, because no bobwhite
were counted or the route was not run that year. Tuesday's "routes leave the data" point is
visible at a glance. But glmer() needs the long version, with year and count as
variables. Both are useful; only one is tidy for modeling.

For anyone fast:

    bw_wide |>
      pivot_longer(cols = -route, names_to = "year", values_to = "count",
                   values_drop_na = TRUE)

Without values_drop_na, every empty cell becomes a row with count NA:
`r big(nrow(bw_back))` rows instead of the original `r big(nrow(bobwhite_counts))`.
(year also comes back as text, because it came from column names;
mutate(year = as.numeric(year)) fixes it.)

Without route, nothing says which row a count belongs to, so pivot_wider()
warns "Values from count are not uniquely identified; output will contain
list-cols" and packs every year's counts into one cell. That warning almost
always means an ID column is missing.

id_cols is not needed here: by default, every column not named in names_from
or values_from identifies the row, which leaves route.
:::

# Pseudocode and comments

## Pseudocode: plan before you code {.smaller}

Write the **steps** in plain words, as comments, **before** writing any code.

- Forces you to think through the **whole** approach first
- Breaks a big job into **small steps you can search for** ("dplyr largest value")
- Stays in the script as its **comments**

. . .

**Which species has the largest beak length difference (culmen minus nares) for
its body mass?**

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Calculate difference in beak lengths (culmen vs nares)
# Divide difference by body mass
# Identify largest mass-corrected difference in beak lengths
```

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. Pseudocode works in any language, and it is how experienced
programmers start anything longer than a few lines. It is also exactly what to
paste into a search engine or a chatbot, one step at a time (Tuesday).

The culmen is measured from the tip to where the beak meets the skull; the
nares measurement is from the tip to the nostrils.
:::

## Then fill it in {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
avo |>
  # Calculate difference in beak lengths (culmen vs nares)
  mutate(delta_beak_length = Beak.Length_Culmen - Beak.Length_Nares) |>
  # Divide difference by body mass
  mutate(mass_corrected_delta_beak_length = delta_beak_length / Mass) |>
  # Identify largest mass-corrected difference in beak lengths
  slice_max(order_by = mass_corrected_delta_beak_length, n = 1) |>
  select(Species1, Family1, mass_corrected_delta_beak_length)
```
:::

**Check:** *`r beak_top$Species1`*, a hummingbird (`r beak_top$Family1`).

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. Each comment became one line of code, and the comments stay as
documentation. A tiny bird with a long beak wins: Myrtis fanny is the
purple-collared woodstar of the Andes.
:::

## Your turn: the most pointed wings {background-color="#f0f4f8" .smaller}

**Which bird family has the most pointed wings, on average, among families with
at least 10 species?**

::: {.type-it}
```{r}
#| eval: false
# first, your pseudocode: three or four steps, as comments

# then fill in the code under each comment
# (hints: group_by(), summarise(), arrange(desc()); after group_by(),
#  n() counts the rows in each group)
```
:::

**Check:** pointiest **`r pointy$Family1[1]`**, mean HWI
`r round(pointy$mean_hwi[1])`. Bluntest: **`r tail(pointy$Family1, 1)`**,
`r round(tail(pointy$mean_hwi, 1))`. `r nrow(pointy)` families qualify.

::: {.notes}
Ten minutes, in pairs. Do not let them skip the pseudocode; the point is the
habit. One version:

    # Group the species by family
    # Keep families with at least 10 species
    # Average each family's hand-wing index
    # Sort from most to least pointed
    avo |>
      group_by(Family1) |>
      filter(n() >= 10) |>
      summarise(mean_hwi = mean(Hand.Wing.Index, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
      arrange(desc(mean_hwi))

Swifts (Apodidae) feed, and some even sleep, on the wing; hummingbirds come
second. Penguins (Spheniscidae) come last, because their "wings" are flippers.
For anyone fast: why does the 10-species cut matter? (Tuesday's small
families: a one-species family's average is mostly luck.)
:::

## Comments: say why {.smaller}

The code already says **what**. Comments should say **why**.

| Says what (the code already did) | Says why (only you know) |
|---|---|
| `# log the mass` | `# log the mass: it runs from 2 g to 111 kg, and lm() wants even scatter` |
| `# remove rows` | `# drop the 2004 counts: the observer changed mid-season` |
| `# use glmer.nb` | `# glmer.nb: the Poisson put only 82% of counts inside its 95% range` |

- Comments also **turn off** code for a moment: Ctrl+Shift+C (Cmd+Shift+C)
- Good "why" comments are **your Methods section**, nearly written

::: {.notes}
Three minutes. The questions worth answering in a comment: why this decision,
why this package and not another, why these rows were excluded. Those are also
what a reviewer asks and what you will have forgotten by the time you write
the paper.

How I work: I write the Methods by copying my comments out of the script, in
order, and then turning them into sentences.
:::

## A workflow that works {.smaller}

1. Start a new script, with a comment at the top saying **what it is for**
2. Write the **pseudocode**, as comments
3. Fill in the **code** under each comment, a section at a time
4. Add comments for each **decision**: why this, and not something else
5. **Restart R and run it all**, top to bottom
6. Use the comments to write the **Methods**

::: {.notes}
Two minutes. Step 5 is the reproducibility check: Session > Restart R, then
Source (Ctrl+Shift+S, or Ctrl+Shift+Enter to see the output). If the script
only worked because of something you typed in the console an hour ago, this is
where you find out, not when I run it.
:::


The rest of the class, at least fifteen minutes. Walk around. Step 6 is the one
that matters most for grading: a script that does not run from a fresh session
loses its reproducibility points.

or to today's hawks.R.
:::

## Which tool, when {.smaller}

| You want to | Use |
|---|---|
| find style problems in a file, or a folder | `lint("file.R")`, `lint_dir("folder")` |
| fix spacing and indentation automatically | `style_file("file.R")`, `style_dir("folder")`, or Ctrl+I |
| jump around a long script | sections: Ctrl+Shift+R |
| one row per measurement (for plotting, `group_by()`) | `pivot_longer()` |
| one row per subject (for reading, or a table) | `pivot_wider()` |
| plan code you do not yet know how to write | pseudocode, as comments |
| make your Methods easy to write | comments that say why |
| prove your script runs | Restart R, then run it all |
